title: Chapter 48
paragraphs: Elinor now learnt the difference between expecting an unhappy event, however certain one tells oneself it is, and knowing it has happened. She discovered that, despite herself, while Edward remained unmarried she had always entertained a hope that something would prevent his marriage to Lucy. Some decision of his own, some intervention by friends, or some better prospect for Lucy might have appeared to make everyone happier. But now he was married. She blamed her heart for the hidden hope that made the news so much more painful.

At first she was a little surprised that he had married so quickly, before, as she supposed, he could have been ordained and therefore before taking possession of the living. But she soon understood how likely Lucy was, in her concern for her own interests and haste to secure him, to ignore everything except the risk of delay. They were married, married in London, and now hurrying to her uncle’s. What had Edward felt at coming within four miles of Barton, seeing her mother’s servant, and hearing Lucy’s message!

She supposed they would soon settle at Delaford. Delaford: a place in which so much combined to interest her, which she wanted to know and yet wished to avoid. Instantly she pictured them in their parsonage. Lucy would be an energetic, calculating housekeeper, combining the wish for a smart appearance with the strictest economy, ashamed to have half her saving practices suspected. Every thought would pursue her own interest, every attention seek the favour of Colonel Brandon, Mrs. Jennings, and each wealthy friend. In Edward she did not know what she saw or wished to see. Happy or unhappy, no picture satisfied her. She turned from every imagined version of him.

Elinor hoped that someone they knew in London would write to announce the marriage and give more details. But day followed day without letter or news. She could not be sure anybody was at fault, yet blamed every absent friend. They were all thoughtless or lazy.
“When will you write to Colonel Brandon, Mama?” she asked, driven by impatience for something, anything, to be happening.
“I wrote last week, my dear. I rather expect to see him before hearing from him again. I urged him warmly to come and should not be surprised if he walked in today, tomorrow, or any day.”
That was something gained, something to anticipate. Colonel Brandon _must_ have at least some news to tell.

She had scarcely decided this when a man on horseback caught her eye through the window. He stopped at their gate. A gentleman—Colonel Brandon himself! Now she would hear more, and she trembled at the prospect. But it was _not_ Colonel Brandon. Neither his height nor his bearing matched. If such a thing were possible, she would have to call him Edward. She looked again. He had just dismounted. There could be no mistake: it _was_ Edward. She moved away and sat down. “He has come from Mr. Pratt’s expressly to see us. I _will_ be calm. I _will_ control myself.”

A moment later she realised the others had discovered their mistake too. Her mother and Marianne changed colour, looked towards her, and whispered a few words together. She would have given anything to speak and make them understand that she wanted no coldness, no slight, in their treatment of him. But no words came. She had to leave everything to their judgement.
Nobody spoke aloud. They waited silently for their visitor. His footsteps sounded on the gravel path. A moment later he was in the passage; another, and he stood before them.

Even Elinor could not consider him too happy as he entered. He was pale with agitation, and looked afraid of his welcome, as though conscious he deserved no kind reception. But Mrs. Dashwood, hoping to follow the wishes of the daughter whose feelings her affectionate heart now intended to consult in everything, greeted him with forced pleasantness. She gave him her hand and offered her congratulations.

He blushed and stammered an incomprehensible reply. Elinor’s lips had moved along with her mother’s. Once the moment had passed, she wished she too had shaken hands with him. It was too late now. Trying to look open and friendly, she sat down again and talked about the weather.

Marianne had withdrawn as far out of sight as possible to hide her distress. Margaret understood part of the situation, though not all. Believing dignity required it, she sat as far from him as she could and said nothing at all.

When Elinor had finished expressing pleasure in the dry weather, a dreadful silence followed. Mrs. Dashwood ended it by feeling obliged to hope he had left Mrs. Ferrars in good health. He hurriedly answered that he had.
Silence followed again.
Determined to make an effort, though frightened by the sound of her own voice, Elinor now asked,
“Is Mrs. Ferrars staying at Longstaple?”
“At Longstaple!” he repeated in surprise. “No. My mother is still in London.”
“I meant,” Elinor said, picking up some work from the table, “to ask after Mrs. _Edward_ Ferrars.”
She dared not raise her eyes. Her mother and Marianne both looked at him. He coloured, seemed confused, glanced uncertainly about, and after some hesitation replied,
“Perhaps you mean—my brother—you mean Mrs.—Mrs. _Robert_ Ferrars.”

“Mrs. Robert Ferrars!” Marianne and her mother repeated in utter astonishment. Elinor could not speak, but even _her_ eyes fixed on him with the same eager wonder. He got up and went to the window, apparently at a loss what to do. Picking up a pair of scissors lying there, he began cutting their sheath to pieces as he spoke, damaging both it and the scissors. In a hurried voice he said,
“Perhaps you don’t know. Perhaps you haven’t heard that my brother recently married—to the younger—to Miss Lucy Steele.”
Everyone echoed his words in indescribable amazement except Elinor. She remained sitting with her head bent down over her work, so agitated that she scarcely knew where she was.
“Yes,” he said, “they were married last week. They are at Dawlish now.”

Elinor could remain seated no longer. She almost ran from the room. As soon as the door closed, she burst into tears of joy which at first seemed as though they would never stop. Until then, Edward had looked anywhere except at her. He saw her hurry away, and perhaps saw, or even heard, her emotion. Immediately afterwards he sank into thought so deeply that no comment, question, or affectionate remark from Mrs. Dashwood reached him. At last he left without a word and walked towards the village. The others remained astonished and bewildered at a change in his circumstances so sudden and extraordinary. They had nothing but their own guesses to explain it.
